content: 1. Bicillin C-R and Bicillin C-R 900/300, which contain penicillin G benzathine and penicillin G procaine, are administered intramuscularly at a dose of 2 million units. The dose should be repeated every 2-3 days until the patient’s temperature has normalized for at least 48 hours. For severe infections, other forms of penicillin, such as intravenous formulations, are required. 2. In patients with a creatinine clearance (CrCl) of 10-50 mL/min, the dose should be reduced by 25%. For those with a CrCl of less than 10 mL/min, the dose should be reduced by 50-70%. Hemodialysis removes the drug, so it should be administered after dialysis sessions. 3. Penicillin G benzathine and penicillin G procaine are indicated for moderately severe to severe infections of the upper respiratory tract, scarlet fever, erysipelas, and skin and soft tissue infections caused by Group A streptococci. These agents are not suitable for treating pneumococcal meningitis. 4. Bicillin C-R is administered as 600,000 units intramuscularly, with the same dosing interval and temperature normalization criteria as above. Bicillin C-R 900/300 is given as 900,000 units/300,000 units intramuscularly, with similar dosing guidelines. These formulations are not defined for pediatric use; adult recommendations should be followed. 5. Penicillin G benzathine can increase the levels or effects of baricitinib by reducing its elimination. Co-administration with strong organic anion transporter 3 (OAT3) inhibitors is not recommended. Alternative drugs should be considered. 6. Ceftobiprole medocaril sodium may increase the levels or effects of penicillin G procaine by inhibiting OATP1B1/1B3 transporters. This interaction necessitates avoiding co-administration or using alternative drugs. 7. Co-administration of penicillin G benzathine or penicillin G procaine with the cholera vaccine results in pharmacodynamic antagonism. Systemic antibiotics may act against the vaccine strain, reducing its efficacy. Cholera vaccination should not be administered to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 8. Lenolisib, an OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 inhibitor, may increase systemic exposure to penicillin G benzathine. This interaction requires avoiding co-administration or using alternative drugs. 9. Penicillin G procaine and penicillin G benzathine can reduce the efficacy of oral microbiota products due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antibiotic regimens should be completed 2-4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. 10. Tetracyclines, such as omadacycline and sarecycline, may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillins, including penicillin G benzathine and penicillin G procaine. This interaction necessitates avoiding co-administration or monitoring for reduced therapeutic effects. 11. Trofinetide, an OATP131 and OATP13B inhibitor, may increase plasma levels of penicillin G benzathine. Co-administration with sensitive substrates should be avoided. 12. Penicillin G benzathine and penicillin G procaine may increase the toxicity of amifampridine, which can cause seizures. Therapy should be modified, and patients should be closely monitored, especially when co-administered with drugs that lower the seizure threshold. 13. Apalutamide may decrease the levels or effects of penicillin G benzathine by increasing its elimination. This interaction requires caution and close monitoring. 14. Penicillin G benzathine and penicillin G procaine may interfere with the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as atezolizumab, avelumab, balstilimab, camrelizumab, cemiplimab, cosibelimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, retifanlimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab. These interactions necessitate caution and close monitoring. 15. Penicillin G benzathine and penicillin G procaine may reduce the efficacy of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering colonic bacterial flora required for drug activation. Caution and monitoring are advised. 16. Penicillin G benzathine and penicillin G procaine may increase the levels or effects of vadadustat by inhibiting OAT1/OAT3 transporters. This interaction requires close monitoring for rapid hemoglobin response and adverse reactions. 17. Penicillin G benzathine and penicillin G procaine may reduce the efficacy of dienogest/estradiol valerate by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral hormone forms and carries a low risk of contraceptive failure. Additional or alternative birth control methods may be advisable. 18. Serious interactions, such as those with baricitinib and ceftobiprole, require avoiding co-administration or using alternative drugs.
